catalog_quote: 18.3 Factors Determining Stress. Several factors help to determine which syllable or morpheme will be stressed. There is no doubt that the predominant factor is phoneme strength. This includes the phonemes' relationship to one another in syllables, and the relative weight of syllables in keeping or shifting stress. Another factor is what kinds of suffixes are involved. There are ones that are always stressed, stressed ones that can become unstressed and ones with slight stress. There are some that are unstressable, and some unstressed which have stress foisted on them. And there are the catalyst suffixes which force stress on others. ... The final factor is how many and which suffixes are being added to the verb. The more suffixes that are added, the further away from it moves the stress. ... sweep_summary: The sweep for Karkar-Yuri (kark1258, Pauwasi) turned up a single stress-titled item, Price 1981 'Determining stress in Karkar' (SIL archive 31140), which is already the catalog's deciding source and already held on file (copied with scanned and page images into and logged). Read on the page images: sec. 18.2 (ms pp.51-52) gives the default position (stem-initial; last stem syllable under suffixation; else first stressable suffix) and sec. 18.3 (ms p.55) the 'phoneme strength' predominance quoted verbatim in the catalog, so the item confirms the 'segmental' coding; nothing supersedes it. The SIL archive record (www.sil.org/resources/archives/31140, HTTP 200, Subject: Stress, Draft posted 'as is', 55 pp., created 1981) was saved. No other stress/accent/prosody title exists for this language in Glottolog, Semantic Scholar or Crossref; the only wishlist rival, Price 1987 orthography paper, could not be reached (old sil.org URL 404, no Wayback snapshot per archive.org/wayback/available, web.archive.org unreachable from our machine, pnglanguages.sil.org and www.sil.org search pages Cloudflare 403)

[...] Front and back vowels (strong) are more likely to take stress than central vowels (weak). [...] If stress cannot shift within the verb stem when suffixes are added, it will rest on the first stressable suffix. [...] There is no doubt that the predominant factor is phoneme strength. This includes the phonemes' relationship to one another in syllables, and the relative weight of syllables in keeping or shifting stress.

new_statements.reading: Stem-initial default with segmentally driven (vowel/consonant 'strength') placement and morphological shifts toward the stem-final syllable or first stressable suffix; a few contrastive pairs and pervasive exceptions. This is the catalog's own deciding source, and the reading supports the 'segmental' coding; the sec. 18.2 sentences are the clearest first-hand statement of position and are already cited in the record as secondary locators.

sources.note: Dedicated 55-page impressionistic study of Karkar word/phrase stress by the SIL fieldworker. Default position is the first syllable of the stem; under suffixation stress prefers the last stem syllable or, failing that, the first stressable suffix; the predominant determinant is 'phoneme strength' (front/back vowels strong, central vowels weak; strong consonants, esp. Cw; closed syllables), with suffix class and number of suffixes as secondary factors; 'contrastive stress on a few words' (erer/e'rer etc., PDF p.4) and many admitted exceptions ('in most cases, stress can be predicted', ms p.51)…
